feedback: If the prediction was 'the fat will feel cold / make no difference', revisit after observing: the fat-protected hand stayed warmer because it trapped your hand's heat.
Reinforce: a coat does not warm a snowman because a snowman makes no heat of its own — insulation only keeps in heat a body already produces.
Ask where the trapped warmth came from, to confirm the body (not the fat) is the heat source.
activities.intendedInsight: Blubber does not generate heat; it insulates, slowing the escape of the body's own warmth — much like how a fat layer protects a seal in cold water.
learnerActions: Make a 'blubber glove': put one zip bag inside another, fill the gap between them with solid vegetable fat (shortening), seal it, and slide one hand into the inner bag; for the other hand, use the same two-bag setup with no fat.
Before testing, PREDICT which hand will stay warmer in iced water and write a reason first.
With an adult supervising, put both hands into a bowl of iced water for a short time and OBSERVE which hand starts to feel cold sooner.
EXPLAIN what happened: did the fat make heat, or trap the hand's own warmth?
Run it as a fair test: change only one thing (fat vs no fat) while keeping everything else the same.
activities.title: Blubber-glove investigation (predict–observe–explain)

feedback: Full understanding: explains blubber and air-trapping fur as insulation that slows the loss of the body's own heat, and matches each other feature to its own challenge (counter-current flippers save heat, the white coat camouflages as well as insulates, migration avoids the harshest season).
Partial: names several adaptations but calls them 'warm/hot' rather than insulating, or can't match a feature to its specific challenge — revisit the blubber-glove result.

Gap: thinks fat/fur makes heat, or explains survival as 'getting used to it' — reteach insulation-vs-heating with the coat-on-a-snowman image, and point to the physical kit (fat, fur, blood-flow) that does the work rather than habituation or willpower.

On the fur-vs-blubber probe, treat it as discussion: underwater, fur's trapped air can be compressed or soaked and lose insulation, while a fat layer still insulates when wet — reasonable but condition-dependent, so accept well-reasoned answers rather than one fixed 'rule'.
activities.intendedInsight: Insulation traps and slows the loss of the body's own heat; it is not a heat source. The animal's body is the heat source and the adaptations keep that heat in.
learnerActions: Consider: a seal swims in near-freezing water for hours and stays warm; a polar bear naps on the ice. A student says 'their thick fat and fur must be really warm — like tiny built-in heaters that make heat to warm the animal up.'
Decide whether the blubber and fur are actually MAKING heat or DOING something else, and explain how they keep a polar animal warm.

Answer the deeper probes: If you wrapped a lump of fat around something that makes no heat, like an ice cube or a snowman, would the fat warm it up? What does that tell you about what blubber is doing? Where does the warmth that blubber traps come from? Why might blubber work better than fluffy fur for an animal that lives IN cold water? Name the two different ways an Arctic fox's white coat helps.
activities.title: Diagnostic: making heat or doing something else?
